correctness.rationale: The complete independent-edge conductance optimization is strictly convex on connected allocations. Right-side vertex symmetry then forces one conductance a_i per left vertex, and connectedness forces all a_i>0. Unit-current calculations establish every pair-resistance type and exact reduced objective. Its positive-definite Hessian proves uniqueness. Its KKT equations give a positive shift alpha with a strictly monotone scalar equation, and substituting proves the optimal value. The unique-minimum large-q expansion uses K_q/q^2 -> 1 and bounded nonminimal contributions. SymPy verifies the exact K_3,4 resistance identity; 96 spectral, 96 KKT, 2400 asymmetric feasible, and four independent full-edge numerical comparisons corroborate. Residual risk: mistakes in source interpretation or a proof algebra step, not resolved by finite comparisons alone.

broader_coverage.reasoning: General strictly convex optimization covers the existence, uniqueness, and implicit KKT equations on arbitrary graphs. It does not expressly provide the one-dimensional exact biclique allocation or the cheapest-row concentration limits. Chen–Yan 2021 concerns pair resistances in product-vertex-weighted networks and is relevant to the pairwise formula but no allocation theorem appears in the abstract. Full text remains unverified; this is a residual risk rather than proof of absence.

value.rationale: Different per-left-vertex conductance prices occur naturally when a network provider or sensor source has its own unit installation cost. The exact optimum is unique against all pq independent edge weights, characterized by a scalar root with a rigorous uniqueness interval and computable optimum. The positive endogenous shift is a structural correction to tree inverse-square-root sizing. For fixed p and expanding q, the proof identifies exact q^{-2} conductance scales on nonminimal-price vertices and asymptotic concentration of the entire budget on a single cheapest vertex; the limiting allocation is not a trivial fixed-size cost substitution. Limit: no assertion about fully arbitrary per-edge prices.
